# Writing That Scales: Design Docs, Decision Records and Runbooks

Last verified: 2026-10-28 against Nygard's 2011 ADR post, Malte Ubl's "Design Docs at Google", and the SRE Book (monitoring, example postmortem). `doclint.py` and the model ADR and runbook were re-run; the lint output matches. Runbook layout, PR template, doc-review questions and the 700-word threshold are labelled as the author's own.

Starts from: lesson 06-staying-agile-through-pivots (decision logs) and lesson 07-shipping-and-operating-precisely (runbooks, postmortems). Nothing else.

## The problem and why it matters

A decision made in a call and never written down gets made again: when a new person joins, when someone forgets, when the person who knew is asleep and the pager rings. Each repeat costs minutes or days. Writing is the way to make a decision once.

My argument for writing (reasoning, not a study): written work lets teammates in other time zones act without you, shortens onboarding, and lets reviewers judge a design before code exists. It is often cheaper than the meetings it replaces.

AI tools draft prose in seconds, so in my view accuracy is now the scarce part. This lesson covers which document to write when, a template for each, and how to own what you publish.

## First principles

1. **Pick the document for the job.** A *design doc* is written before building, to settle an ambiguous design. An *ADR* (architecture decision record) records one decision and its reasons. A *runbook* is read during an incident: step-by-step help for a known symptom. A *PR description* tells a reviewer what changed and how to check it. A *postmortem* (lesson 07) is written after an incident.
2. **Write for a reader with no context.** Assume they are smart, new, tired and hurried. Define terms on first use, put the conclusion first, and link instead of retelling history.
3. **Not every change needs a design doc.** Malte Ubl's "Design Docs at Google" says the decision turns on whether the solution to the design problem is ambiguous; if it is not, "there is little value in going through the process of writing a doc". His test is five questions (unsure of the design? would senior reviewers help? ambiguous or contentious? does the team sometimes forget cross-cutting concerns like privacy, security or logging? is there a need for high-level docs of a legacy system?); if you answer yes to "3 or more", a design doc is "probably a great method" to start with.
4. **A design doc has a shape.** Ubl lists: context and scope (objective background facts; "This isn't a requirements doc"), goals and non-goals ("things that could reasonably be goals, but are explicitly chosen not to be goals"), the design (where trade-offs are written down), alternatives considered, and cross-cutting concerns. The template below adds summary, decision, risks, rollout and open questions, which are my additions.
5. **An ADR is short and permanent.** Michael Nygard's 2011 post gives five parts: Title (a short noun phrase), Context (the forces at play, in value-neutral language), Decision ("stated in full sentences, with active voice", beginning "We will"), Status ("proposed" if stakeholders have not agreed, "accepted" once they have; later "deprecated" or "superseded") and Consequences (positive, negative and neutral effects). The whole document "should be one or two pages long", numbered sequentially and monotonically (numbers are not reused), and kept in the project repository. Nygard writes: "If a decision is reversed, we will keep the old one around, but mark it as superseded." Why it matters is my gloss: knowing what was decided and why still helps later readers.
6. **A runbook is symptom, check, action, escalate.** This four-part layout is a teaching format, not a standard. The reader arrives with a symptom (an alert name), needs one cheap check to confirm, one safe action, and a clear point to hand off. It must be linked from the alert that pages. The SRE book says every page should be actionable; a runbook is one way to make that true (my framing).
7. **Use AI to draft, but you own every claim.** An AI draft can state a wrong number or an invented source in the same confident tone as a right one. Before publishing, check every number, name, link and command against its source, delete what you cannot verify, and put your name on it. Your name is the guarantee.
8. **Review a doc like code.** (My advice.) Ask what is unclear, missing, assumed, and what would fail. Review the decision, not the prose style.

## How it works

### Which document, and when

```
 idea ---> design doc ---> build ---> ship ---> incident
              |              |         |           |
              v              v         v           v
            ADR(s)       PR descr.  runbook   postmortem
          one decision   per change  per alert  + actions
              |                        ^           |
              +--- links ----> docs <--+-----------+
```

### The context ladder

```
 reader's question          where it is answered
 +------------------+     +----------------------+
 | what is this?    | --> | title + 1st sentence |
 | do I care?       | --> | summary (3 lines)    |
 | what should I do?| --> | decision / ask       |
 | why this way?    | --> | options + tradeoffs  |
 | how do I check?  | --> | rollout, tests       |
 +------------------+     +----------------------+
```

Put the answers in that order and a busy reader can stop at any rung and still know what you meant.

### Templates

```markdown
# Design doc: <noun phrase>
Author / Reviewers / Status (draft, in review, accepted) / Date

## Summary (3 lines: problem, proposal, ask)
## Context and scope (objective background; define terms)
## Goals
## Non-goals (reasonable goals we are choosing not to pursue)
## Options considered (each: how it works, pros, cons, cost to reverse)
## Decision and why (link the ADR)
## Cross-cutting concerns (security, privacy, observability, cost)
## Risks and mitigations
## Rollout and rollback plan (stages, metrics, who watches)
## Open questions (owner, due date)
```

```markdown
# ADR <n>: <short noun phrase>
Status: Proposed | Accepted (date) | Superseded by ADR <m>
## Context (forces at play, value-neutral)
## Decision (We will ...)
## Consequences (good, bad and neutral)
```

```markdown
### Symptom: <what the alert or user sees> (alert: <name>)
Check: <one cheap command or dashboard that confirms it>
Action: <the safe first step; say what to do if the check differs>
Escalate: <who, when (a time limit), and how>
```

```markdown
## What and why (2-3 sentences; link the issue or spec)
## How to review (where to start; what is risky)
## How I tested it (commands run, output seen, what I did not test)
## Rollout and rollback (flag? migration step? how to undo)
## AI assistance (what a tool drafted; what I verified myself)
```

### Demo: lint your docs

A **linter** is a program that checks files against rules. This one checks that an ADR has the parts above and that each runbook entry has Check, Action and Escalate. It cannot judge quality, only completeness. Save as `doclint.py`.

```python
"""Doc lint: does an ADR or runbook have the parts a reader needs?"""
import re
import sys

def lint_adr(text):
    problems = []
    if not re.match(r"# ADR \d+: \S", text):
        problems.append("title must look like '# ADR 7: Short noun phrase'")
    for part in ("Status:", "## Context", "## Decision", "## Consequences"):
        if part not in text:
            problems.append(f"missing {part}")
    if "We will" not in text:
        problems.append("decision should say 'We will ...' in active voice")
    if len(text.split()) > 700:
        problems.append("longer than ~2 pages (heuristic: 700 words)")
    return problems

def lint_runbook(text):
    problems = []
    entries = re.split(r"^### ", text, flags=re.M)[1:]
    if not entries:
        problems.append("no '### Symptom' entries found")
    for entry in entries:
        name = entry.splitlines()[0]
        for field in ("Check:", "Action:", "Escalate:"):
            if field not in entry:
                problems.append(f"entry '{name}' has no {field}")
    return problems

if __name__ == "__main__":
    failed = False
    for path in sys.argv[1:]:
        kind = lint_adr if path.startswith("adr") else lint_runbook
        found = kind(open(path).read())
        failed = failed or bool(found)
        print(f"{path}: {'ok' if not found else 'PROBLEMS'}")
        for p in found:
            print(f"  - {p}")
    sys.exit(1 if failed else 0)
```

```text
# captured here on macOS (python3 doclint.py <3 files>)
adr-009-dead-letter-queue.md: ok
runbook-queue-backlog.md: PROBLEMS
  - entry 'Symptom: dead-letter queue is not empty (alert: dlq-nonempty)' has no Escalate:
adr-bad.md: PROBLEMS
  - title must look like '# ADR 7: Short noun phrase'
  - missing Status:
  - missing ## Context
  - missing ## Decision
  - missing ## Consequences
  - decision should say 'We will ...' in active voice
exit 1
```

The ADR and runbook below (a hypothetical incident and decision) are the model answers to this lesson's exercise. In the first draft of the runbook, the second entry had no Escalate line, and the lint caught it; the blocks below include the fix, and after it the same command printed `ok` for both files and exited 0. `adr-bad.md` was a two-line file ("We decided stuff") included to show what the lint rejects.

### Exercise and model answer

**Task:** take lesson 07's failure scenario (a consumer crash-looping on a message with a missing field) and write (a) a runbook entry and (b) an ADR. Try yours first, lint it, then compare.

```markdown
# ADR 9: Park repeatedly failing messages in a dead-letter queue
Status: Accepted (2026-10-28)

## Context
A message with a missing field crashed the consumer on every attempt.
The consumer restarted, read the same message and crashed again, so
everything behind it waited. Only API errors had alerts, so nobody
knew for hours. We want one bad message to cost one message, not the
whole line. Parking messages hides data problems unless someone is
told, so parking needs its own alert.

## Decision
We will move any message that fails 3 times to a dead-letter queue
(a side queue for messages that keep failing) and keep consuming.
We will alert when the dead-letter queue is not empty and when the
oldest message in the main queue is older than 5 minutes.

## Consequences
- Good: one bad message no longer blocks others.
- Good: failures are kept for inspection and replay.
- Bad: messages can be processed out of order after a replay.
- Bad: a new queue and two alerts to own and keep documented.
- Neutral: the retry count of 3 is a guess; revisit after one month.
```

```markdown
### Symptom: oldest queued message age is rising (alert: queue-age)
Check: Is the consumer restarting? A rising restart count means a
crash loop. Check the logs for the last error and whether it repeats
on the same message id.
Action: If a deploy went out in the last day, roll it back first and
watch the age fall. If no deploy, move the repeating message to the
dead-letter queue and restart the consumer once.
Escalate: If age still rises 15 minutes after the action, page the
owning team and open an incident.

### Symptom: dead-letter queue is not empty (alert: dlq-nonempty)
Check: Read one parked message and its error.
Action: If it is malformed input, file a bug with the producer.
Escalate: If the same error type arrives within a day, page the
producer team.
```

The "3 times", "5 minutes" and "15 minutes" values are examples chosen for the exercise, not recommendations; pick yours from your own traffic and SLO.

## Worked failure scenario

**Symptom (hypothetical):** on-call follows the runbook for "queue backlog": "restart the consumer". They restart it three times over 40 minutes and the backlog keeps growing.

1. **Is the runbook current?** Its last edit is eight months old. It predates the dead-letter queue and the current consumer.
2. **Did the check distinguish cases?** It had no Check step, so on-call could not tell "consumer stuck" from "consumer crash-looping on one message".
3. **Escalation.** It named no time limit, so nobody escalated until the third restart failed.
4. **Fix the entry:** add the Check (restart count, repeating message id), a branch (rollback or park the message) and a 15-minute escalate rule.
5. **Fix the system:** the alert links directly to the entry, and an ADR records why parking exists so nobody removes it as clutter.
6. **Prevent rot:** the responder updates the entry in the same pull request that closes the action item; each entry has an owner and a "last verified" date.

## Tradeoffs

| Use when | Avoid when |
|---|---|
| Design doc for ambiguous, contentious or cross-team designs (Ubl's 3-of-5 test) | The design is obvious and small; a PR description is enough |
| ADR for any decision someone will later ask "why" about | Reversible, trivial choices (naming a variable) |
| Runbook for every paging alert | Alerts that are not actionable; fix the alert instead |
| AI-drafted text for first drafts and restructuring | Facts, numbers or citations you have not checked yourself |

## Interview questions

1. When do you write a design doc and when not? *Probe:* how would you judge? *Outline:* ambiguity and contention; Ubl's five questions, 3 or more yes; skip for obvious work.
2. What is an ADR and how do you handle a reversed decision? *Outline:* Title, Context, Decision, Status, Consequences; mark superseded, never delete.
3. What goes in a runbook entry, and why link it from the alert? *Outline:* symptom, check, action, escalate with a time limit; the pager reader has no time to search.
4. How do you make a PR easy to review? *Outline:* what and why, how to review, how tested and what was not, rollout and rollback.
5. How do you use AI for writing responsibly? *Outline:* draft only; verify every claim; disclose; own it.
6. How do you review a design doc? *Outline:* missing alternatives, hidden assumptions, undefined terms, no rollback, vague non-goals.

**Whiteboard exercise:** write one ADR for a decision you made this month. Lint it with `doclint.py`, then hand it to a colleague who was not in the room and ask them to say back what was decided and why. Fix every place they hesitate.

## Checklist

1. I can choose the right document for a situation.
2. I can fill the design doc, ADR, runbook and PR templates.
3. Every runbook entry has symptom, check, action and escalate with a time limit.
4. I verify every number, name and link in AI-drafted text before publishing.
5. I write the conclusion first and define terms on first use.
6. I can review a doc for missing alternatives, assumptions and rollback.

## Common wrong answers

- "Code is the documentation." It rarely shows why, or what was rejected.
- "Write a design doc for everything." That is slow ceremony.
- "Edit the old ADR when we change our minds." Supersede it instead.
- "The AI wrote it, so the AI is responsible." You published it.
